issues.subcategory: Meta-analysis of correlations appears incorrectly specified
issues.description: The manuscript states that metafor's rma function was given effect-size r and N parameters. Meta-analysis of correlations normally requires transforming correlations to Fisher's z and using the correct sampling variance, then back-transforming; rma does not simply take raw r and N as sufficient inputs for a valid inverse-variance meta-analysis. If raw r values or sample sizes were used directly as inputs/weights, the pooled estimates, standard errors, CIs, p-values, heterogeneity estimates, and prediction intervals may be incorrect.
issues.quote: The rma function was used, which accepts the effect size r and N parameters (syntax is available on the OSF page https://osf.io/r659c/).

issues.subcategory: Equating standardized beta with correlation without sufficient qualification
issues.description: The note states that effect-size r is equivalent to the standardized beta coefficient. This is only true in a simple bivariate regression with exactly one predictor, identical cases, and no covariates or weighting. The manuscript does not clearly document the exact regression specification and missing-data handling for each study, making this equivalence potentially unsafe. It is also contradicted by the original advantageous-disclosure values reported elsewhere.
issues.quote: Note. Beta coefficients are standardized (consistent with the original research). Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: Original advantageous-disclosure effect size is inconsistent across manuscript
issues.description: The original effect for advantageous self-disclosure is reported as -.30 in the abstract/results table but as -.33 in Table 3 and the discussion. These values are not interchangeable, and the stated p-value does not align cleanly with either value for N = 80. Because the original effect size is the benchmark for replication comparisons, this inconsistency directly affects interpretation of whether replications were smaller or consistent with the original.
issues.quote: Self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30) / Original | Forest & Wood | Forest & Wood | 80 | n/a* | .181 |  | -.220 | .050 |  | -.310 | .005 |  | -.300 | .011 / BYU-Sp16 | -0.02 | -0.33 | -0.31

issues.subcategory: Non-significant meta-analytic result described as significant
issues.description: For opportunity to connect, the results report a meta-analytic p-value of .065 and a 95% CI including zero, but the discussion says the meta-analytic effect was significantly different from zero. This is a direct statistical contradiction and changes the substantive conclusion for one of the four focal outcomes.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065. / However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number for expression differs between results and discussion
issues.description: The results state the fail-safe number for opportunity to express self was 3 studies, but the discussion says it was five unreported studies. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the reported robustness assessment.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies. / The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number for connection differs between results and discussion
issues.description: The results state the fail-safe number for opportunity to connect was 5 studies, whereas the discussion reports 11 studies. This inconsistency affects interpretation of the stability of the connection finding.
issues.quote: The FSN was 5 studies. / These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).

issues.subcategory: Safety prediction interval reported inconsistently
issues.description: For self-disclosure safety, the results report a 95% prediction interval of [-.54, -.03], but the discussion reports [-.40, -.15], which appears to be the confidence interval rather than the prediction interval. Confusing CI and PI materially changes claims about expected effects in future studies, especially because prediction intervals address between-study variability.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was -.28, 95% CI [-.40, -.15], 95% PI [-.54, -.03], p < .001. / The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.

issues.subcategory: Absence of significant individual effects treated as evidence of no effect despite significant meta-analysis
issues.description: For opportunity to express self, the manuscript concludes that self-esteem did not relate to the outcome because all individual replication CIs included zero, yet the meta-analysis is reported as statistically significant with a CI/PI excluding zero. Non-significant individual studies do not establish absence of effect, and a significant pooled estimate contradicts the stated conclusion of no relationship.
issues.quote: Self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero). / the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero, and the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number misused to support null conclusions
issues.description: Fail-safe N estimates how many unpublished null results would be needed to make a statistically significant meta-analysis non-significant; it is not evidence that an effect is absent. The manuscript uses a small FSN for expression to support confidence in a lack of effect even though the pooled effect is reported as statistically significant. This is a misuse of the statistic.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: Fail-safe number reported for a non-significant meta-analysis
issues.description: The methods define FSN as applicable to significant meta-analytic results, but an FSN is reported and interpreted for the opportunity-to-connect meta-analysis even though its p-value is .065. Applying FSN to a non-significant result is not meaningful under the stated rationale.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis was intended to identify the number of non-significant, unreported studies required to add to the meta-analysis to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance. / The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065. / The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.subcategory: Publication-bias inference not justified by replication effect sizes
issues.description: The discussion infers publication bias in the original study from smaller replication effects and prediction intervals. A single original study cannot be diagnosed as affected by publication bias merely because later estimates are smaller; differences could reflect sampling error, temporal changes in Facebook use, procedural deviations, measurement differences, or population differences. Publication bias is a literature-level selection process, not something demonstrated by one original-replication discrepancy.
issues.quote: the summary effect size was about half of the original’s effect size, and the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study’s, all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study.

issues.subcategory: Overinterpretation of p-values just below .05
issues.description: The manuscript suggests that p-values between .04 and .05 are relatively more likely under the true null than under a false null. This claim is not generally valid without specifying prior probabilities, power, effect-size distributions, and the sampling/selection process. It risks dismissing the original connection finding based on an overgeneralized p-value heuristic.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that the original study obtained a p-value of .05, and p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.subcategory: Borderline p = .050 treated as significant without clarification
issues.description: The original connection result is described as significant even though the table reports p = .050. Depending on rounding and the prespecified alpha rule, p = .050 may or may not meet a p < .05 criterion. The manuscript should report the exact p-value and clarify the decision rule rather than treating it unambiguously as significant.
issues.quote: Original | Forest & Wood | Forest & Wood | 80 | n/a* | .181 |  | -.220 | .050 |  | -.310 | .005 |  | -.300 | .011 / Contrary to the results of the original study, six of the seven replication studies did not find self-esteem to be a significant predictor of opportunity to connect.

issues.subcategory: Prediction intervals interpreted too strongly
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly states that prediction intervals show what future studies would find. A random-effects prediction interval is an interval for the true effect in a new comparable setting, not a guarantee about observed effect sizes in 95% of future studies; with only seven studies, prediction intervals are also highly uncertain. The overstatement inflates confidence in future replication outcomes.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14 / The PI came close to, but did not include, zero so it may be that there is an effect

issues.subcategory: Random-effects inference with very small number of studies may be anti-conservative
issues.description: Only seven studies were meta-analyzed per outcome. Standard REML/Wald-type random-effects tests from metafor can have poor coverage and inflated Type I error with small k unless methods such as Hartung-Knapp or robust sensitivity analyses are considered. This is especially important for marginal effects such as r = .08, p = .021 and r = .09, p = .065.
issues.quote: This meta-analysis synthesized seven direct pre-registered replications / Analyses were conducted using the R package metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010). The rma function was used

issues.subcategory: Effect-size difference signs and labels are ambiguous
issues.description: Table 3 is labeled as replication versus original effect-size comparisons, but the reported differences appear to be original minus replication rather than replication minus original. Without specifying the direction of subtraction, signs are easy to misinterpret, and textual statements such as effects being 'smaller' are confusing when effects are negative or opposite in sign.
issues.quote: Table 3 Replication vs. Original Effect Size r Comparisons / BYU-Sp16 | -0.02 | -0.33 | -0.31 | [ -0.59 , -0.01 ]

issues.subcategory: Meta-analytic model selected using data-dependent interpretability criterion
issues.description: The authors compared REML and DerSimonian-Laird models and selected REML because it produced 'more interpretable' heterogeneity estimates. This is a vague, post hoc, data-dependent criterion. Model choice can affect standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values, and heterogeneity estimates, so it should be prespecified or accompanied by transparent sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

issues.subcategory: No clear preregistration of the meta-analysis itself
issues.description: The manuscript states that individual replication studies were preregistered, but it does not state that the meta-analysis protocol, inclusion/exclusion criteria, effect-size conversions, variance estimators, model choice, prediction intervals, FSN analyses, or sensitivity analyses were preregistered. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom at the synthesis stage.
issues.quote: the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study’s OSF page / This meta-analysis synthesized seven direct pre-registered replications

issues.subcategory: Multiple unadjusted replication-original comparisons
issues.description: The manuscript makes 28 replication-original effect-size comparisons across four outcomes and seven studies using 95% CIs, then interprets counts of significant differences. No multiplicity correction, hierarchy of outcomes, or preregistered decision rule is described. This increases the chance of false-positive claims about individual replications differing from the original.
issues.quote: We also chose to analyze the effect size differences between the original study and each of the replications. / Table 3 shows the effect size differences between the original and replication studies and their 95% CIs.

issues.subcategory: Unexplained study-level attrition from 17 forks to 7 included studies
issues.description: The OSF project had 17 forks, but only seven studies were included. The manuscript does not explain what happened to the other ten forks, whether any collected data but failed to post results, whether exclusions were made blind to results, or whether incomplete/nonposted studies could bias the meta-analysis. This is a study-level missing-data/availability problem.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 “forks” representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process / These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository. All seven studies were included in this meta-analysis.

issues.subcategory: Minimum sample-size statement contradicts included sample sizes
issues.description: The methods state that all studies collected the minimum required number of participants and that the required number was 120, yet the reported sample sizes include 80, 81, 90, 94, and 116. This contradiction makes the inclusion criteria and power planning unclear and raises questions about whether studies actually met CREP requirements.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power) / Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.subcategory: Individual replications underpowered for target effects
issues.description: Several individual studies had N around 80-116, which gives low power for correlations in the range of approximately .15 to .22 and only moderate power for r around .30. The manuscript relies on counts of significant individual replications and replication-original differences, but many studies were too small for such inferences. The authors acknowledge wide CIs, but the design still limits conclusions about failed individual replications.
issues.quote: Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374. / Generally, the sample sizes required for precision in comparing the difference in effect sizes will be larger than for judging simple significance.

issues.subcategory: Procedural deviations undermine claim of direct replication
issues.description: The replications varied in administration mode, setting, group versus individual completion, questionnaire wording/order, and response scale. These deviations can affect self-report responses, privacy, social desirability, measurement distributions, and comparability across studies. They also make it difficult to attribute differences from the original to replicability rather than procedural heterogeneity.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods). Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six. Two other known differences across replications involved minor discrepancies in presentation of the RSE scale

issues.subcategory: Direct and Direct-Plus replications conflated
issues.description: The abstract and methods repeatedly characterize the studies as direct replications, but some were Direct-Plus replications with additional measures. Although the added measures came after the focal measures, the manuscript should consistently distinguish direct from direct-plus designs and document whether participants were aware of the additional tasks or whether any recruitment/instruction differences occurred.
issues.quote: Seven pre-registered direct replication attempts of this study were conducted / Some research teams chose a Direct-Plus replication, and included additional personality-type measures following the primary measures.

issues.subcategory: Non-independence of studies from same institutions/teams not addressed
issues.description: Seven datasets came from only five institutions, with repeated BYU and IIT samples and overlapping authors/teams. Random-effects meta-analysis assumes independent effect-size estimates. Shared institutional context, recruitment pools, procedures, mentors, or analytic practices may induce dependence; no multilevel model or sensitivity analysis by institution/team is reported.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US / BYU-Sp16 | Wiggins, et al. / BYU-Wi17 | Foster, et al. / IIT-Sp16 | Legate, et al. / IIT-Sp17 | Legate, et al.

issues.subcategory: Facebook-user status and use intensity not reported
issues.description: The focal constructs are perceptions of Facebook as a venue for self-disclosure, expression, and connection, but the manuscript does not report whether participants had Facebook accounts, were active users, how often they used Facebook, or whether non-users were excluded. By 2016-2017, Facebook use among college-aged participants varied substantially; including infrequent users or non-users would weaken construct validity and alter generalizability.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017 / Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers

issues.subcategory: Expression and connection measures do not match comparative hypothesis
issues.description: The introduction frames the hypothesis as Facebook being better than face-to-face interactions for self-expression, but the methods describe expression and connection items as assessing only whether Facebook enabled expression/connection, whereas only safety and advantages were explicitly comparative with FTF. This operationalization mismatch weakens conclusions about Facebook relative to face-to-face interaction for expression and connection.
issues.quote: hypothesized that people with low self-esteem would perceive Facebook as a safer place to self-disclose, and a better place to express their emotions with others as compared to FTF interactions / Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others. Perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook compared to in person interactions was measured with nine items. Ten more items assessed perceived advantages of disclosing on Facebook versus FTF.

issues.subcategory: Ad hoc Facebook perception measure has limited validity evidence
issues.description: The Facebook perception measure was created by the original researchers, and this manuscript reports only internal consistency ranges. Internal consistency does not establish construct validity, factor structure, measurement invariance across sites/modes/years, or whether items still captured the same constructs after platform and user-base changes.
issues.quote: Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012). / Subscale scores showed adequate to good internal consistency

issues.subcategory: Perceived benefits conflated with actual benefits or behavior
issues.description: The study measures perceptions that Facebook is safer/advantageous or enables connection/expression, not actual self-disclosure behavior, actual social support, social outcomes, or realized benefits. Several interpretations refer to benefits, use, preferences, or tendencies, which exceed the operationalized constructs.
issues.quote: Self-disclosures on Facebook can be made without some of the immediate indicators of disapproval present in FTF interactions, and thus increase the tendency to self-disclose (Hollenbaugh & Ferris, 2014).  This perspective is supported by the present research.

issues.subcategory: Correlational bivariate design cannot support causal or directional claims
issues.description: The analyses are associations between self-esteem and self-reported perceptions. They do not establish that self-esteem causes perceptions of Facebook, that Facebook mitigates anxiety, or that low self-esteem leads people to use Facebook for compensation. Unmeasured third variables such as social anxiety, depression, loneliness, general social media use, gender, age, and institution could explain the associations.
issues.quote: Effect size r represented the size and direction of the relationship of self-esteem scores to the four outcome variables / We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions

issues.subcategory: No covariate or confounder strategy
issues.description: The regression models appear to use self-esteem as the sole predictor of each outcome. Without prespecified covariates or sensitivity analyses, the study cannot determine whether associations are specific to self-esteem rather than demographic composition, social media use, social anxiety, personality, campus context, or administration mode.
issues.quote: For each of the four outcome variables, we present the standardized beta and p-value for the regressions. / Effect size r represented the size and direction of the relationship of self-esteem scores to the four outcome variables

issues.subcategory: Social compensation theory not directly tested
issues.description: The manuscript says the findings provide support for social compensation theory, but the study did not measure the theory's key mechanisms: anxiety in face-to-face interactions, compensatory motivation, actual online interaction, displacement/substitution, or improved social outcomes. Perceptions of safety/advantages are at most indirect evidence.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000; Wilson et al., 2012). This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions.

issues.subcategory: Missing or incomplete descriptive statistics table
issues.description: Table 2 is referenced as containing demographic and descriptive statistics, but in the provided manuscript it contains only the title and note, with no actual descriptive values. This prevents evaluation of sample composition, scale distributions, possible range restrictions, and cross-study comparability.
issues.quote:
Table 2

Descriptive Statistics for All Replication Studies

Note. n/a = Data not available. n/c = Data not collected

issues.subcategory: Insufficient recruitment and eligibility details
issues.description: The manuscript does not report how participants were recruited, whether they received course credit or compensation, eligibility criteria, whether Facebook users/non-users were screened, whether duplicate participation across semesters was prevented, or whether any attention/quality checks were used. These details are needed to evaluate selection bias and replicability.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017

issues.subcategory: Missing data handling and exclusions not documented
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that not all studies documented missing-data handling, composite-score calculations, or data exclusions. Because effect sizes depend on which cases and items were included, lack of consistent missing-data and exclusion procedures threatens reproducibility and comparability across replications.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: Participant-level missingness not quantified
issues.description: The manuscript does not report the amount of missing item-level or participant-level data, how many participants were excluded per study, whether missingness differed by measure or site, or whether complete-case analysis was used. Without this information, readers cannot assess attrition/missing-data bias.
issues.quote: Data were not always collected or stored consistently (e.g., race collected in some but not all studies; individual item-level data were not always stored).

issues.subcategory: Composite scoring inconsistent or unclear across studies
issues.description: The manuscript notes that some studies apparently mean-averaged scales while Gordon apparently summed items. Although linear transformations do not change simple correlations, inconsistent or undocumented scoring affects descriptive comparability, reliability checks, and reproducibility. It also signals lack of standardized analysis procedures across sites.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: Demographic data incompletely collected
issues.description: Race was collected in only three replications, and other demographic variables were generally not collected because the original article did not report them. This prevents assessment of sample comparability, site heterogeneity, and potential demographic moderation or confounding. Replication fidelity does not justify omitting basic demographics needed to evaluate generalizability.
issues.quote: In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected because the original Forest and Wood (2012) research did not indicate any other demographic information was collected

issues.subcategory: Group administration may affect privacy-sensitive self-report
issues.description: One site administered questionnaires in groups of two to six, whereas others had participants alone or online. Measures concern self-esteem and perceptions of self-disclosure, which may be sensitive to perceived privacy and social evaluation. The group-administration deviation is therefore not obviously minor and was not analytically controlled.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.subcategory: Response-scale changes across studies
issues.description: Two replications used a five-point Rosenberg Self-Esteem scale while most used a four-point scale. Scale changes can alter distributions, reliability, range restriction, and correlations, especially when self-esteem is the predictor in all analyses. The manuscript does not report harmonization procedures or sensitivity analyses excluding these studies.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.subcategory: Question wording/order changes in predictor measure
issues.description: One study changed item order and wording for four of ten Rosenberg Self-Esteem items. Even small wording changes can affect psychometric properties and comparability in a direct replication, particularly when the altered measure is the sole predictor.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., ‘At times I think I am no good at all’ vs. ‘I think I am no good at all’)

issues.subcategory: Broad conclusions from US undergraduate samples
issues.description: All replication samples were US undergraduates, but the manuscript often frames conclusions in terms of Facebook users or individuals generally. College students in 2016-2017 are not representative of Facebook's broader user base by age, country, culture, socioeconomic status, or usage patterns. General claims should be restricted accordingly.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US / We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions

issues.subcategory: Temporal and platform-change limits to direct replication
issues.description: The original study was published in 2012, whereas replications were conducted in 2016-2017, after substantial changes in Facebook's user base, features, norms, and competition from Instagram/Snapchat. The manuscript discusses this possibility but still describes the studies as direct replications and draws conclusions about Facebook generally. Temporal instability is central for social-media constructs.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017 / Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others

issues.subcategory: Conflation of different connection/expression constructs across studies
issues.description: The manuscript compares its perceived opportunity-to-connect/expression measures with another study's 'acquaintance-related functions' and uses differences to speculate about cultural moderation. These are not the same constructs or operationalizations, so divergent signs may reflect measurement differences rather than cultural or platform effects.
issues.quote: Their study found a significant negative relationship (r = -.11) between self-esteem and using Facebook for acquaintance-related functions (e.g., being known by others and meeting new people), suggesting that those lower in self-esteem used Facebook for connection and expression. This finding runs contrary to the results of our meta-analysis

issues.subcategory: Insufficient reporting of item-level materials and psychometrics in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript provides only ranges of reliability coefficients and does not reproduce the Facebook perception items, exact response anchors, per-study alphas, factor structure, or item-level descriptive information. Referring readers to OSF is helpful, but the article itself lacks enough information to evaluate measurement quality and replication fidelity.
issues.quote: Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others. Perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook compared to in person interactions was measured with nine items. Ten more items assessed perceived advantages of disclosing on Facebook versus FTF. / Subscale scores showed adequate to good internal consistency

issues.subcategory: Inclusion criteria depend on posted results, not just posted data
issues.description: The inclusion rule required studies to have posted data and results. Conditioning inclusion on posted results rather than on preregistered initiation or data availability can introduce bias if teams with incomplete, null, problematic, or unfavorable results were less likely to post. The manuscript does not explain whether searches for unposted data or team follow-up were conducted.
issues.quote: These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository. All seven studies were included in this meta-analysis.

issues.subcategory: Equivalence/null goals dismissed but null-like conclusions made
issues.description: The authors state that goals involving null effects and equivalence were not applicable because they did not expect null findings. However, they later make conclusions that self-esteem does not relate to self-expression and that results are consistent with the original null finding. Claims of no effect or equivalence require appropriate equivalence/null-focused analyses, not merely non-significant tests.
issues.quote: We did not develop these studies expecting a null finding, so goals (2) and (6) are not presently applicable. / The replications supported the original study’s finding that self-esteem was not a significant predictor of perceptions that Facebook provided opportunities to express the self
